question: to the Commission Ewa Zajączkowska-Hernik (PfE) Subject:

In the draft Council recommendations to Poland for 2026-2027, the Commission points to the challenges women face in terms of pension poverty and pursuing STEM careers. What gets overlooked, however, are the systemic problems boys and men face in terms of educational inequalities, vocational training and labour market segmentation. The omission of official data on the marginalisation of men therefore gives rise to concerns about the objectivity of the Commission’s analyses and hints at an ideological approach. Irrespective of the criticism levelled at the role played by the European Semester and Council country-specific recommendations within the EU architecture, these documents should be drawn up in an impartial and fair manner. Against this background: 1.
How does the Commission explain the failure to reference problems affecting boys and men, despite the data available in this regard?
Will it supplement the recommendations or introduce the obligation for a balanced analysis of the situation of both genders in subsequent European Semester cycles?

What role did the Member States play in drawing up the recommendations pertaining to gender equality standards, and how did the Commission take the position of the Polish authorities into account when drawing up these recommendations?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.8.2026) Country-specific recommendations are based on challenges identified in the country reports. The 2026 country report for Poland notes that gender disparities in employment are high. The gender employment gap is 1.6 percentage points above EU average. In 2023, women accounted for only 17% of tertiary students and 17.5% of professionals in the field of information and communication technology. The report highlights challenges affecting both women and men, including the low efficiency of vocational education and training, which limits graduate outcomes. Employment among graduates declined from 82.3% in 2022 to 76.9% in 2025. Labour market segmentation is identified as a general challenge. The Commission continuously monitors relevant data using Eurostat and other official indicators. The framework is reviewed by the relevant subgroups of the Council’s consultative committees1 to ensure that developments affecting different demographic groups are adequately reflected providing for an evidence-driven assessment, considering inequalities and countryspecific contexts. In line with Articles 121 and 148 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, the Commission draws up recommendations for the Council on economic, social, employment and budgetary issues based on the country reports, which were consulted with Member States and considering their requests and comments. After publication, the recommendations are examined by the relevant Council preparatory bodies and Member States’ delegates2. Amendments are proposed before finalisation and submitted to the Council. The comments of Member States were considered throughout the process. The Council adopted the texts of the recommendations on 10 July 2026 and are now final3.
1 The Indicator Group of the Employment Committee and the Indicator Subgroup of the Social Protection

Committee. 2 The Economic and Financial Committee, the Economic Policy Committee, the Employment Committee, and the Social Protection Committee. 3 https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-11133-2026-INIT/en/pdf.
